newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Hong Kong diesel stocks brimming, ships turned away.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong diesel stocks brimming, ships turned away.

text.p: A large build up of diesel stocks in Hong Kong has led some major oil companies there to turn away cargoes that were originally destined for re-sale to China, industry sources said on Friday.
"Hong Kong majors turned away some cargoes due to slow sales to China," one trader said.
"The cargoes are not flowing as much as anticipated earlier. The buying spree (from China) is over," said a source at an oil major with large trading interest in China.
These cargoes are mainly from their own refinery system in Asia and the Middle East that were subsequently absorbed by the oil majors, the trader said.
The Hong Kong market is dominated by five major oil companies that own and operate large terminals with a total storage capacity of more than 700,000-tonnes, sources said.
Oil companies that have terminals there include Shell, Esso, Mobil, Caltex, a joint venture between Chevron Corp and Texaco Inc, and China Resources Co.
As a result of the slump in Chinese demand, diesel prices have plummeted to $210 per tonne on an ex-terminal Hong Kong basis, from a peak of about $280 per tonne in early December.

The collapse was precipitated by price falls of similar magnitude in Singapore where diesel nosedived to trade this week at $25.20-$25.40 per barrel from a peak of $34.45 per barrel in early December, both on a free-on-board (fob) basis.

The Hong Kong market is a key transit point for sales of small barge lots of diesel to China. At the height of Chinese demand in December the terminals were selling between 20 and 30 barges daily to barge operators.
These barges have the capacity to ship between 1,000 and 5,000 tonnes each.
Due to earlier high turnover, the Hong Kong terminal operators, expecting demand to remain at the high level, ordered similar amounts for second half January and February arrival.
But demand from China came to a virtual standstill during mid-January.
"We have not moved very much (cargoes) in the past few days," the source said.
The sources said one tanker carrying about 50,000-tonnes of diesel waited one week before it was able to discharge part of its cargo.
The demurrage costs were so high the tanker was forced to sail to Singapore with part of its cargo unsold, the source said.
Most players said the market is not likely to recover until after the Lunar New holidays at the end of next week when Chinese buyers return to the market.
China's huge appetite for diesel is the key to any price recovery in the region, traders said.
It bought up to one million tonnes of diesel a month for arrival in December and January, but has bought less than half this amount for February.
